concepts.title: The Node.js Event Loop & libuv
concepts.description: Node.js executes your JavaScript on a single thread, yet routinely serves thousands of concurrent connections without a thread per request. The event loop and the libuv library underneath it make this possible, and understanding them explains both Node's biggest strength and its most common performance trap.
learningObjectives: Explain why Node.js can handle many concurrent I/O-bound operations despite running your JavaScript on a single thread.
Describe the role libuv and its thread pool play in offloading work that has no native asynchronous OS API.
List the event loop's main phases -- timers, poll, and check -- and identify what kind of callback runs in each.
Distinguish blocking (synchronous) calls from non-blocking (asynchronous) calls, and predict which one will stall every other request being served.
Predict the relative ordering of setTimeout, setImmediate, and process.nextTick callbacks in a given snippet.

sections.heading: One Thread, Many Connections
sections.body:
Your JavaScript in a Node.js process runs on one thread: one call stack, one thing executing at a time (worker threads, covered below, are the opt-in exception). If that were the whole story, Node would be a poor choice for a server, because a web request that took even 200ms to handle would make every other concurrent client wait behind it. That isn't what happens, because Node separates 'running your JavaScript' from 'waiting on I/O.' When your code calls a database query, a file read, or an HTTP request to another service, Node doesn't spin the CPU waiting for the answer. It hands the request off to the operating system's networking stack or to libuv (covered below) and returns control to your thread, which can handle another incoming request, run a timer, or respond to a different client. When the I/O operation finishes, its result is placed on a queue, and the event loop picks it up and runs your callback on that same thread at the next opportunity.

This is why Node is described as good at I/O-bound workloads and bad at CPU-bound ones. A server that spends most of its time waiting on a database, a disk, or another network service can have hundreds of those waits in flight at once, because waiting costs no CPU time on your thread; it happens outside your JavaScript. A server that spends its time computing (resizing images, running a complex regex over megabytes of text, computing a hash) has no such trick, because that work runs as JavaScript on your one thread and nothing else can run meanwhile. For CPU-heavy work the fix is not to study the event loop harder but to move the work off the main thread, using worker_threads (a separate JS thread with its own event loop), a child process, or another service. The event loop doesn't parallelize CPU-bound code; it only ensures that code doesn't block anyone unless you write it in a way that does.

sections.heading: libuv and the Thread Pool
sections.body:
The event loop itself, plus a good deal of what makes non-blocking I/O possible, is implemented by a C library called **libuv**, which Node is built on top of. libuv gives Node two strategies for turning slow operations into non-blocking ones, and which one applies depends on the kind of operation. This trips up people who assume 'async I/O' is one uniform mechanism.

For network I/O -- TCP sockets, which is what HTTP servers and most databases sit on top of -- the operating system provides asynchronous, event-driven APIs (epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS/BSD, IOCP on Windows). libuv uses these to ask the OS to notify it when a socket has data ready, and does something else in the meantime. No extra thread is created per socket; the kernel handles the waiting, and libuv collects whatever is ready during the event loop's poll phase (see the next section).

File system operations are a different story. Most operating systems' file APIs are blocking at the OS level, and on most platforms there is no epoll-style 'tell me when this file read is done' as there is for sockets. So for fs operations (and a handful of others: crypto functions like pbkdf2 and scrypt, DNS lookups via dns.lookup, and some zlib compression calls), libuv gets non-blocking behavior by handing the blocking call to a **worker thread pool**: a fixed-size pool of background OS threads, four by default, controlled by the UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE environment variable. The call blocks one of those background threads (not your main JS thread), and when it finishes, its result is queued back for your callback to run on the main thread.

The practical consequence: the thread pool is small (four threads by default) and shared by every fs/crypto/dns/zlib operation your app issues. If you start twenty crypto.pbkdf2 password hashes at once, only four run in parallel; the other sixteen queue for a free thread while your main JS thread sits idle. This is a confusing performance cliff ('my server has plenty of idle CPU cores, why are my password hashes queuing up?'), and the answer is usually that the libuv thread pool size, not the core count or the main thread, is the bottleneck for that class of operation.

sections.heading: The Phases of the Event Loop
sections.body:
The event loop is not one undifferentiated queue. It's a fixed cycle of **phases**, each responsible for a category of callback, run in the same order every iteration of the loop. The phases that matter most day to day are:

1. **timers**: runs callbacks scheduled by setTimeout and setInterval whose delay has elapsed. The delay is a minimum, not a promise: if the loop is busy, the callback runs late.
2. **pending callbacks**: runs certain I/O callbacks deferred from the previous loop iteration (mostly some error cases you'll rarely touch).
3. **poll**: the workhorse phase. It retrieves new I/O events (a socket became readable, a file read finished) and runs their callbacks. If nothing else is scheduled, the loop sits here and blocks waiting for something to happen instead of spinning the CPU, which is why an idle Node process uses roughly 0% CPU while still serving connections.
4. **check**: runs setImmediate callbacks, *after* the poll phase has finished for this iteration.
5. **close callbacks**: runs close-event handlers, e.g. socket.on('close', ...).

One detail explains much of the 'why did that run in that order' confusion: **process.nextTick and resolved Promises are not phases of the event loop.** They are drained from separate queues *between every callback*, not just between phases. The nextTick queue is checked and fully drained first, then the Promise microtask queue, and only when both are empty does Node move on to the next callback in the current phase or the next phase. That's why process.nextTick(fn) and Promise.resolve().then(fn) run before *any* timer or I/O callback, however small a delay you give setTimeout: they cut in line ahead of the phase-based loop every time.

A classic ordering puzzle for building intuition is setTimeout(fn, 0) vs setImmediate(fn) called at the top level of your program (not inside an I/O callback). Their order is **not guaranteed** there, because it depends on process startup timing that varies from run to run. Call them from *inside* an I/O callback, such as an fs.readFile callback (which runs during the poll phase), and the order becomes deterministic: setImmediate always fires first, because the loop is already in the poll phase, proceeds to the check phase next (running the setImmediate callback), and reaches the timers phase only on the *next* iteration.

sections.heading: Blocking vs Non-Blocking I/O, and Why Blocking Is the Cardinal Sin
sections.body:
Every core I/O API in Node ships in (at least) two flavors: a blocking, synchronous version, usually suffixed Sync (fs.readFileSync, fs.writeFileSync), and a non-blocking, asynchronous version (fs.readFile with a callback, or fs.promises.readFile). The synchronous version blocks: the single JS thread stops and waits, doing nothing else, until that operation completes. No other request is served, no timer fires, no other callback runs; the whole process is frozen for the duration of the call.

That's reasonable in a one-off script or during startup before you accept traffic: reading a config file synchronously before app.listen() is fine, because there's no concurrent traffic to stall yet. It becomes a serious bug inside code that runs *per request* in a server meant to serve many clients: one client's request stalls every other client's for as long as the synchronous call takes, defeating the concurrency model the runtime is built around. It's one of the most common ways Node servers get slow under load, and it's often invisible in local testing with one browser tab open, because with only one client there's nothing else waiting to be blocked.

'Non-blocking' refers to I/O: waiting on a network response, a disk read, a timer. It does **not** mean 'safe from stalling the loop.' A synchronous, CPU-heavy computation, such as a JSON.parse of a multi-megabyte payload, a regular expression suffering catastrophic backtracking, or a tight loop over a large array, blocks the event loop as thoroughly as fs.readFileSync does, and there is no asynchronous version of 'do less CPU work.' The fix for I/O is the non-blocking API; the fix for heavy computation is to make it faster, break it into chunks that yield back to the event loop, or move it off the main thread with worker_threads. To see whether something is blocking the loop, measure event loop delay (perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay() reports how late callbacks are running); steadily rising delay under load means something synchronous is hogging the thread.

examples.title: Blocking the Event Loop with a Synchronous Call
examples.explanation: If one client requests /report while a large file is being read synchronously, every other client, even one hitting the cheap '/' route, waits for the whole read to finish, because there is one thread and it's occupied. A single manual test with one browser tab looks fine, since nothing competes for the thread; the problem appears only under concurrent load, which is why this class of bug so often reaches production. The fix is to swap fs.readFileSync for fs.readFile (callback) or fs.promises.readFile (awaited in an async handler); either lets the event loop keep serving other requests while libuv's thread pool does the disk read in the background.

examples.title: setImmediate vs setTimeout Inside an I/O Callback
examples.explanation: Both calls happen inside an I/O callback, which runs during the poll phase, so the ordering is deterministic, unlike the same two calls at the top level of a script. Once the poll phase finishes this callback, the loop moves on to the check phase, where setImmediate's callback is waiting, and runs it. Only on a *later* pass through the cycle does the loop reach the timers phase, where the setTimeout callback gets its turn. So 'immediate' always prints before 'timeout' here because of where in the phase cycle the surrounding code runs; the same two calls outside an I/O callback have no such guarantee.

examples.title: process.nextTick, Promises, and setTimeout: Full Ordering
examples.explanation: All synchronous code runs to completion first, top to bottom, before any queued callback gets a turn, so 'start' and 'end' print first, in that order, whatever was scheduled between them. Once the synchronous code finishes, Node fully drains the process.nextTick queue before looking at the Promise microtask queue, so 'nextTick' prints next. Only when that queue is empty does Node drain the microtask queue, printing 'promise'. Only when *both* queues are empty does the event loop move into the timers phase and run the setTimeout callback, printing 'timeout' last. The order (nextTick, then microtasks, then the phase-based event loop) is fixed and worth memorizing, since it's the source of most 'why did this run before that' surprises. One caveat: this output is for a CommonJS file. In an ES module the top-level code itself runs inside a promise job, so 'promise' prints before 'nextTick'.

misconceptions.description: Node.js being 'single-threaded' means it can only ever do one thing at a time, including I/O -- so lots of concurrent requests must secretly be queued up and handled one after another.
misconceptions.clarification: JavaScript execution is single-threaded, but I/O work is delegated to the operating system's asynchronous facilities or to libuv's thread pool, both of which run concurrently outside that one JS thread. Only the (typically tiny) work of running your callback when an I/O operation finishes is scheduled onto the single thread, one callback at a time. That's why a server juggling many slow database calls can still feel snappy: the waiting doesn't consume your thread's time, and your thread is free to handle other callbacks in the meantime.
misconceptions.fact: JavaScript execution is single-threaded, but I/O work itself is delegated to the operating system's asynchronous facilities or to libuv's thread pool, both of which genuinely run concurrently, outside that one JS thread entirely.

misconceptions.description: setTimeout(fn, 0) means fn runs immediately, essentially at time zero, ahead of anything else.
misconceptions.clarification: Node clamps the minimum timer delay to 1ms, but that isn't the main point. 'Immediately' in the strongest sense, before anything else, is closer to what process.nextTick does than to setTimeout. Whatever delay you pass, a setTimeout callback waits for the current synchronous code to finish, for the process.nextTick queue to drain, for the Promise microtask queue to drain, and for the event loop to reach the timers phase. Even process.nextTick doesn't preempt running synchronous code; it jumps ahead of timers and I/O callbacks once that code finishes.

exercises.prompt: What does this print, and in what order? Explain why.
hints: Synchronous code (anything not inside a callback) always finishes first, top to bottom, before any queued callback gets a turn.
Once the synchronous code is done, Node fully drains the process.nextTick queue before it even looks at the Promise microtask queue.
Only after both the nextTick queue AND the microtask queue are completely empty does the event loop move on to the timers phase, where the setTimeout callback is waiting.
exercises.expectedAnswer: 1: start, 5: end, 4: nextTick, 3: promise, 2: timeout -- in that order.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The two console.log calls outside any callback ('1: start' and '5: end') are plain synchronous code, so they run first, in the order they appear, whatever gets scheduled between them. Once that code finishes, Node drains the process.nextTick queue completely, so '4: nextTick' prints next. Only after that queue is empty does Node drain the Promise microtask queue, printing '3: promise'. Only when both queues are empty does the event loop enter the timers phase and run the setTimeout callback, printing '2: timeout' last.

exercises.prompt: This HTTP server is meant to serve an instant response on '/' even while a slower '/report' request involving a large file read is in flight for another client. In testing with two simultaneous clients, the '/' request is unexpectedly delayed until the '/report' request finishes. Find and fix the bug.
hints: While fs.readFileSync blocks, who else is affected besides the client that requested /report?
Node has more than one API for reading a file. Which one lets the event loop keep handling other requests while the read is in progress?
Look for a callback-based or Promise-based fs API, and remember your handler function itself will need to become async (or accept a callback) to use it.
exercises.solutionExplanation: fs.readFileSync blocks the single JS thread for the duration of the read, and while it runs nothing else can happen, including handling the concurrent '/' request. Switching to fs/promises's readFile (non-blocking, handled by libuv's thread pool) and awaiting it inside an async request handler lets the event loop keep servicing the '/' request, and everyone else, while the '/report' read happens in the background. The main thread re-engages with that request only once the data is ready, which is the concurrency model Node is designed around.

assessments.prompt: A Node.js server issues twenty concurrent crypto.pbkdf2 password-hashing calls (a CPU-heavy operation Node routes through libuv's thread pool). The machine has 16 idle CPU cores. What should you actually expect?
options: All twenty run fully in parallel immediately, since there are far more CPU cores than operations.
They run one at a time, always, because pbkdf2 blocks the event loop directly.
Only as many run in parallel as there are threads in libuv's thread pool (four by default).
None of them can run until the main JS thread is completely idle, since libuv borrows the main thread for CPU-heavy work.
assessments.explanation: libuv's thread pool defaults to four threads (controlled by UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE), and that pool size, not the number of CPU cores, limits operations routed through it, so at most four of the twenty pbkdf2 calls run in parallel at any moment; the rest queue for a free thread. The “All twenty run fully in parallel immediately…” option is wrong because idle cores don't matter unless UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE is raised to use them. The “None of them can run until…” option is wrong: the thread pool is separate from the main JS thread and doesn't need it to be idle. The “They run one at a time, always…” option is wrong because pbkdf2 is one of the operations libuv offloads to the thread pool *so that* it doesn't block the event loop, and the pool allows four at once.

assessments.prompt: Node's TCP/network I/O does not need libuv's worker thread pool, while file system operations do. What actually explains this difference?
options: File system operations are handled directly in the poll phase, bypassing the thread pool entirely, while network operations always use the thread pool.

Operating systems provide genuinely asynchronous, event-driven APIs for sockets (epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS/BSD, IOCP on Windows) that libuv can hook into directly, but most OS file APIs are fundamentally blocking, so libuv offloads those calls to background threads in the pool instead.
Node maintains a separate, larger thread pool exclusively for network sockets that isn't governed by UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE.
Network I/O is inherently faster than disk I/O, so it never needs a background thread regardless of the OS.
assessments.explanation: The difference comes down to what the operating system offers. For sockets, the OS provides non-blocking, event-driven notification, so libuv asks to be told when a socket is ready and does other work meanwhile, with no extra thread. Most file APIs have no equivalent 'notify me when ready' mechanism, so libuv gets non-blocking behavior for fs calls by running the blocking call on a background thread from its fixed pool. The “Network I/O is inherently faster than disk…” option is wrong: relative speed isn't the mechanism. The “Node maintains a separate, larger thread pool…” option is wrong: there is no socket-specific pool, and sockets don't need the thread pool. The “File system operations are handled directly…” option is wrong: it inverts which category uses the thread pool.

assessments.prompt: An I/O callback is currently running during the poll phase. Partway through, it calls process.nextTick(fn) once. Relative to the event loop's next callback (whether that's the next poll-phase callback or the check phase), when does fn actually run?
options: Immediately after the current callback finishes, before the event loop moves on to anything else at all -- process.nextTick's queue is drained between every single callback, not just between phases.
Only on the next full iteration of the event loop, after every phase has had a turn.
Only after the poll phase entirely finishes and the check phase begins.
At a genuinely unpredictable time, since nextTick provides no ordering guarantee relative to other callbacks.
assessments.explanation: process.nextTick's queue (and the Promise microtask queue right after it) is drained between every callback, not merely between the event loop's phases, so fn runs as soon as the current I/O callback finishes, before the loop proceeds to whatever callback would normally run next, even one in the same poll phase. The “Only after the poll phase entirely finishes…” and “Only on the next full iteration…” options both describe a phase-based or iteration-based deferral, which nextTick bypasses. The “At a genuinely unpredictable time, since nextTick…” option is wrong: nextTick's ordering relative to other callbacks is a fixed guarantee.

assessments.prompt: A developer replaces a blocking fs.readFileSync call with fs.promises.readFile inside a request handler, but the server still stalls under concurrent load whenever a request triggers JSON.parse on a very large payload already in memory. What best explains this?
options: Switching to fs.promises.readFile made things worse, because it always runs on a separate thread that contends with JSON.parse for CPU time.
fs.promises.readFile doesn't actually use libuv's thread pool, so it's just as blocking as the Sync version was.
The event loop's poll phase automatically blocks whenever any JSON parsing occurs, regardless of payload size.
JSON.parse is itself a synchronous, CPU-bound operation running entirely on the main JS thread.
assessments.explanation: 'Non-blocking' refers to I/O (waiting on a disk, a network response, a timer), not to CPU-heavy computation. A large JSON.parse is ordinary synchronous JavaScript that runs to completion on the main thread, blocking every other request as thoroughly as a synchronous I/O call, and switching the file read to a non-blocking API changes nothing, since the read was never the bottleneck here. The “fs.promises.readFile doesn't actually use libuv's thread pool…” option is wrong: fs.promises.readFile is non-blocking. The “The event loop's poll phase automatically blocks…” option is wrong: the poll phase has no special blocking behavior tied to JSON parsing. The “Switching to fs.promises.readFile made things worse…” option is wrong: its I/O work happens in the thread pool, while the CPU-bound JSON.parse still runs on the main thread.

assessments.prompt: A teammate says: 'Node.js is single-threaded, so our server can only truly handle one request at a time -- the concurrency everyone talks about is really just an illusion created by interleaving.' Explain what's right and what's misleading about this claim, using the event loop and libuv to justify your answer.
assessments.modelAnswer: The narrow part of the claim is true: JavaScript execution in Node is single-threaded, and at any instant only one JS callback is running. Where the claim goes wrong is in equating 'running JS' with 'handling a request.' For a typical I/O-bound request (one that queries a database, reads a file, or calls another service) most of its wall-clock lifetime is spent waiting, not computing, and that waiting is delegated to the operating system's asynchronous socket facilities or to libuv's thread pool, both of which run concurrently outside the JS thread. So hundreds of requests can be 'in flight', waiting on their own I/O, at almost no cost to the JS thread, which is needed only for the small slices of work each request requires: parsing input, deciding what to do, building a response. Those slices run one at a time, interleaved by the event loop, but they're small relative to the waiting time, so for I/O-bound workloads the system behaves like real concurrency, and the single JS thread is rarely the busy resource. The teammate's framing becomes correct for CPU-bound workloads: if a request needs substantial computation, there's nothing to delegate, and that computation runs to completion on the one thread, blocking every other request. That's why CPU-heavy work should be moved to worker_threads or a separate process rather than handled inline.

assessments.prompt: An Express API's latency spikes to several seconds for every user whenever one customer exports a large report, even though the server's CPU has several cores. Explain the cause and how to fix it.
assessments.modelAnswer: Node runs JavaScript on a single main thread driven by the event loop. If the export does heavy synchronous work, such as building a huge JSON string, CSV formatting in a tight loop, or synchronous file and crypto calls, it blocks the loop, so no other request callbacks run until it finishes and every user waits. Extra cores do not help because one process uses one JavaScript thread. Fixes: move CPU-heavy work to worker_threads or a separate job queue and worker service, stream the report to the client (or to storage) in chunks instead of building it in memory, and avoid *Sync APIs in request paths. Run several processes behind a load balancer to use all cores. Monitor event loop lag (for example with perf_hooks monitorEventLoopDelay) so blocking is detected early.

concepts.title: Callbacks, Promises, and Async/Await in Node
concepts.description: Node's asynchronous story evolved in three layers: error-first callbacks, then Promises, then async/await syntax on top of Promises. All three schedule work through the same event loop, but they differ sharply in how errors propagate, how well they compose, and how easy it is to write a subtly broken program.
learningObjectives: Write and correctly consume a Node-style error-first callback, checking the error argument before touching any result.
Explain what 'callback hell' actually costs beyond indentation -- specifically around error handling and composability.
Convert a callback-based API to a Promise-based one using util.promisify, and know when a Promise-native version already exists.
Use async/await with try/catch to write asynchronous logic that reads top-to-bottom, and explain what an async function actually returns.
Identify the bug caused by forgetting to await a Promise inside an async function, including how it can produce an unhandled promise rejection.

sections.heading: The Original Pattern: Error-First Callbacks
Callback Hell Costs More Than Indentation
Promises: A Value That Represents a Future Result
sections.body:
A **Promise** is an object representing a value that may not exist yet, but will (eventually) either resolve successfully or reject with an error. A Promise is in one of three states at any moment: **pending** (still waiting), **fulfilled** (resolved with a value), or **rejected** (failed with a reason). Once it leaves pending, it never changes state again. You attach a handler for the eventual success value with .then(value => ...), for the failure with .catch(err => ...), and for 'run this regardless of outcome' with .finally(() => ...). Handlers always run asynchronously, even on an already-resolved Promise.

The key improvement over raw callbacks is that .then() calls **chain**, and a single .catch() at the end catches a rejection from *any* earlier step, so you don't need an error check at every level:

```javascript
const fs = require('fs/promises');

fs.readFile('./user-id.txt', 'utf8')
  .then(id => db.getUser(id.trim()))
  .then(user => db.getOrders(user.id))
  .then(orders => fs.writeFile('./orders.json', JSON.stringify(orders)))
  .then(() => console.log('Done.'))
  .catch(err => handleError(err));
```

This reads top to bottom as a flat pipeline instead of a nested pyramid, and one .catch() handles a failure from *any* of the four steps, so an error can't slip through the way a missed if (err) check could. For code that still exposes an old-style callback API (in Node core or an older third-party library), util.promisify(fn) wraps it into a function that returns a Promise, assuming it follows the standard (err, result) convention. Most of Node's own core modules now ship a Promise-based variant (fs.promises, or require('node:fs/promises')), so util.promisify is increasingly needed only for older third-party callback APIs.

sections.heading: async/await: The Same Promises, Read as Straight-Line Code

examples.title: Correctly Consuming an Error-First Callback
examples.explanation: The if (err) return; guard matters: if the file doesn't exist, err is an Error object and contents is undefined. Without the guard, the code falls through to JSON.parse(undefined), which throws an unrelated-looking error (in Node 24, '"undefined" is not valid JSON'; older versions said 'Unexpected token u in JSON at position 0') that says nothing about the root cause, a missing file. Misleading messages like that make callback code painful to debug. Checking err first and returning means the real cause is what gets reported.

examples.title: Fixing an Unhandled Rejection Caused by a Missing await
examples.explanation: Because await is missing, user is bound to the Promise object that db.getUser(userId) returns, not to the eventual user record, so user.orders is undefined (Promises have no orders property), and reading .length off that throws a TypeError on the next line. Here the mistake surfaces fairly loudly because getUserOrderCount's returned Promise rejects and the caller has a .catch() that logs it. If nothing had attached a .catch() or try/catch to the call chain, the same TypeError would become an unhandled promise rejection, which on modern Node terminates the process instead of printing a warning. The fix is to add the missing await in front of db.getUser(userId).

examples.title: Sequential vs Parallel awaits with Promise.all
examples.explanation: Both functions are valid async/await code with no missing awaits, and they produce the same array of results. The difference is timing: the sequential version's for...of loop awaits each call before starting the next, so three network round trips happen back to back. The parallel version calls db.getOrders for every id with no awaiting in between, so all three requests are in flight the moment the function runs, and Promise.all waits for the slowest. When the operations are independent, the sequential version wastes wall-clock time for no correctness benefit; if a later request depended on an earlier one's result, sequential awaiting would be the only correct option. (Firing everything at once can also overload a database or API, so for large id lists, batch the work or limit concurrency.)

misconceptions.description: Marking a function async makes it run on a separate thread, in parallel with the rest of the program.
misconceptions.clarification: async is Promise syntax sugar only: it introduces no new threads and no new concurrency mechanism. An async function's synchronous statements execute on the single main thread, in order, like any other function. Execution appears to 'jump away' because an await pauses that function and hands control back to the event loop, which may run something else while waiting. Concurrency comes from I/O operations yielding control back to the event loop, never from the async keyword creating threads or running your JS in parallel.
misconceptions.fact: async is Promise syntax sugar only -- it introduces no new threads and no new concurrency mechanism.

misconceptions.description: await pauses the entire program -- it blocks the event loop until the Promise resolves.
misconceptions.clarification: await only suspends the one async function it's written in; the event loop keeps running everything else (other timers, other I/O callbacks, other async functions' continuations) while that function waits to resume. It's a local, cooperative suspension of a single call, not a global freeze. If await blocked the whole event loop, it would defeat the purpose of non-blocking I/O and be no better than the Sync functions from the previous concept.
misconceptions.fact: await only suspends the one async function it's written in; the event loop keeps right on running everything else -- other timers, other I/O callbacks, other async functions' continuations -- while that particular function waits its turn to resume.

exercises.prompt: This code tries to fetch a 'user' for each id and log them in order, using Array.prototype.forEach. What does it actually print, and why doesn't it wait for each fetch to finish before starting the next?
hints: forEach calls its callback once per element, but does it do anything with what the callback returns?
The callback passed to forEach here is an async function, so it returns a Promise every time it's called. forEach ignores that return value and never awaits it.

Because forEach fires off all three async callbacks without waiting between them, they all start their timers at about the same moment, so whichever has the SHORTEST delay logs first, not whichever started first.
exercises.expectedAnswer: 'done looping' prints first, followed by 'user-3', 'user-2', 'user-1' in that order (shortest delay first), NOT 'user-1', 'user-2', 'user-3' in id order, and 'done looping' doesn't wait for anything.
exercises.solutionExplanation: forEach invokes its callback once per element but never awaits the Promise an async callback returns, so it fires all three calls back to back with no waiting. Each call starts its own timer (100 - id*10 ms: 90ms, 80ms, 70ms) and forEach returns, so printUsers's body continues to console.log('done looping'), which runs before any timer fires. When the timers complete, the shortest one (id=3, 70ms) resolves first, so 'user-3' logs first, then 'user-2' at 80ms, then 'user-1' at 90ms, the reverse of what a naive reading of the loop suggests. If sequential in-order processing was intended, the fix is a plain for...of loop (which does await each iteration before starting the next); if order doesn't matter but waiting for all of them does, use Promise.all(ids.map(...)).

exercises.prompt: This function is supposed to return the total number of orders across several users, fetched from a slow database call. It's supposed to run all the lookups concurrently, since they don't depend on each other, but profiling shows it takes roughly three times longer than a single lookup for three users -- meaning it's actually running them one at a time. Find and fix the bug.
hints: Look at where await appears relative to the loop. Does the loop start the next iteration's request before or after the current one finishes?
await inside a for...of loop pauses the loop at every iteration; it won't move to the next id until the current db.getOrders call has resolved.
You want to START every request first, all at once, without waiting yet, collect all the resulting Promises, and only then wait for all of them together.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original loop awaits db.getOrders(id) on every iteration, so the next call isn't made until the current one resolves: three sequential round trips, roughly 3x the latency of a single call. The fix separates 'starting' the requests from 'waiting' for them: userIds.map(id => db.getOrders(id)) calls db.getOrders for every id back to back with no awaiting, producing an array of Promises that are all in flight concurrently. Promise.all takes that array and returns a single Promise that resolves once every one has resolved (or rejects as soon as any one rejects), so the total wait is about the duration of the slowest lookup, not the sum of all of them.

assessments.prompt: What does calling an async function that has no explicit return statement, and that never throws, actually give you?
options: A Promise that resolves with the value undefined.
undefined, exactly like a normal non-async function with no return statement.
A Promise that stays pending forever, since nothing was explicitly returned.
A SyntaxError, because async functions require an explicit return statement.
assessments.explanation: An async function always returns a Promise. If it falls off the end without an explicit return <value>, that Promise resolves with undefined, mirroring how a plain function with no return statement evaluates to undefined, except wrapped in a Promise. The “undefined, exactly like a normal non-async function…” option is the answer for the same code without the async keyword; adding async is what changes it. The “A Promise that stays pending forever, since…” option is wrong: falling off the end of a function body is not the same as never settling; the function completes and resolves with undefined. The “A SyntaxError, because async functions require…” option is wrong: async functions may omit return, which is common when the purpose is a side effect rather than a value.

assessments.prompt: Why do Node's core APIs pass an error as the first argument to a callback instead of simply throwing when something goes wrong during an asynchronous operation?
options: Throwing inside an asynchronous callback would work fine; Node's designers preferred passing errors as data purely for stylistic consistency across the API.
JavaScript did not support throw statements inside callback functions until ES2015, so early Node had no choice.

By the time an asynchronous operation actually completes and its callback runs, the original call stack -- including any try/catch that wrapped the initial call -- is long gone, so there is no meaningful place for a thrown error to be caught; passing the error as an argument to a callback guaranteed to run works regardless of timing.
Passing errors as a callback argument avoids the performance cost of constructing an Error object.
assessments.explanation: A synchronous try/catch relies on the calling stack frame still being alive when the error occurs, but an asynchronous callback runs long after the function that scheduled it has returned, so that stack frame and any try/catch around it no longer exist. Node's core APIs sidestep this by handing the error to the one function guaranteed to run when the operation finishes: your callback, as data in its first parameter. The “Throwing inside an asynchronous callback would work…” option misses that there's a technical reason, not just style. The “JavaScript did not support throw statements inside…” option is factually wrong: throw has always worked inside callbacks; the problem is stack lifetime, not syntax. The “Passing errors as a callback argument avoids…” option is not the motivation; the cost of constructing an Error plays no role in the convention.

assessments.prompt: A developer claims: 'Marking a function async makes its body run on a separate thread, so several async functions execute their code in true parallel.' What's wrong with this claim?
options: async functions do run on separate threads, but only during the specific line where an I/O operation is awaited, not during ordinary synchronous statements.
async functions run on libuv's worker thread pool, the same pool used for fs and crypto operations.
Nothing -- this is exactly how async functions behave in Node.
async is Promise syntax sugar only; it creates no new threads.
assessments.explanation: The async keyword only changes what a function returns (always a Promise) and allows await inside its body. It introduces no new concurrency mechanism and no new thread. Every synchronous statement in an async function's body executes on the main JS thread, in order, like any other function; the appearance of 'jumping away' comes from await pausing that one function and returning control to the event loop, which can run other pending work. The “async functions do run on separate threads…” and “async functions run on libuv's worker thread…” options both invent a thread-based mechanism that doesn't exist: await never hands JS execution to another thread. The I/O may be handled elsewhere (by the OS or libuv's pool), but the async function's own JS code runs only on the main thread.

assessments.prompt: On Node 15 and later, what happens by default when a Promise rejects and nothing in the program -- no .catch(), no surrounding try/catch around an await -- ever handles that rejection?
options: Node silently discards the rejection; nothing is logged and the process continues normally.
The process crashes and exits, because Node's default behavior for an unhandled promise rejection changed from merely warning to actually terminating the process.
The rejected Promise is automatically retried up to three times before Node gives up and logs an error.
Node logs a DeprecationWarning to the console, but the process keeps running exactly as it did on older Node versions.
assessments.explanation: Earlier Node versions printed a warning for an unhandled promise rejection and kept running. Starting with Node 15, an unhandled rejection terminates the process by default, on the reasoning that an error nobody was prepared to handle is likely a bug that shouldn't be allowed to fail silently. That's why a single missing await, which can produce an unhandled rejection if the un-awaited Promise later rejects, can become a production crash instead of a warning. The “Node silently discards the rejection; nothing…” and “Node logs a DeprecationWarning to the console…” options describe older or nonexistent behavior; the “The rejected Promise is automatically retried up…” option describes a retry mechanism Promises don't have.

assessments.prompt: Explain, to a developer new to Node, why forgetting the await keyword on a Promise-returning call inside an async function is a common and often dangerous bug, and how the mistake can eventually surface as an 'unhandled promise rejection' crash.
assessments.modelAnswer: When you call a Promise-returning function without await inside an async function, the call still happens and the operation starts, but the variable you assigned is bound immediately to the Promise object, not to the value it will resolve with, because execution didn't pause. Code right after that line that assumes it has the resolved value (reading a property, passing it where a plain object is expected) now operates on a Promise, which typically gives undefined for property lookups or a TypeError, and the error is confusing because it seems to be about a missing property rather than a missing await. The deeper danger comes when that abandoned Promise later rejects. Nothing attached a .catch() or wrapped the (missing) await in a try/catch, so no handler is waiting for the rejection, and it becomes an 'unhandled promise rejection.' In Node 15 and later, the default for this escalated from printing a warning to terminating the process. So a single missing await can go from 'looks like it worked, mostly' in casual testing to a process crash in production when that call happens to reject instead of resolve, an intermittent, hard-to-reproduce failure worth watching for in code review.

concepts.title: CommonJS vs ES Modules
concepts.description: Node shipped its own module system, CommonJS (require/module.exports), years before JavaScript standardized ES Modules (import/export). Node now supports both, but they differ in loading semantics, scoping, and interop in ways that cause specific errors when you mix them carelessly.
learningObjectives: Write and consume a module using both CommonJS (require/module.exports) and ES Module (import/export) syntax.
Explain why require() loads synchronously while import loads asynchronously, and connect that back to when each system was designed.
Configure a project to use ES Modules via package.json's type field or explicit .mjs/.cjs extensions.
Identify which CommonJS-only globals (__dirname, __filename, require) are missing in ESM and how to reconstruct their equivalents.
Diagnose the ERR_REQUIRE_ESM error and other common interop failures when CommonJS and ESM code meet in the same project.

sections.heading: Two Systems, One Runtime
Synchronous Loading vs Asynchronous, Static Loading
sections.body:
require() is a **synchronous** function call. When your code hits require('./math'), Node reads that file from disk right there, executes its top-level code, and returns module.exports, all before your next line runs. Node caches the result, so requiring the same file again returns the same module.exports object without re-running the file, which is also what makes circular requires terminate. This was a reasonable design in 2009: Promises didn't exist yet in JavaScript, and a synchronous 'load and return the value' model is about as simple as a module system gets. A consequence is that you can require() conditionally, inside an if or a function, with a computed string; it's a normal function call that happens to load code.

import, by contrast, is **not** a function call. It's a declaration, and the ES Module system statically analyzes a module's entire dependency graph *before running any module's code*, then resolves and loads everything asynchronously. That's why import statements must appear at the top level of a file (never inside an if or a function) and why specifiers must be literal strings: a tool can work out the complete dependency graph by reading the file without executing anything, which enables optimizations like dead-code elimination ('tree-shaking') in bundlers and lets resolution be asynchronous without your code waiting line by line. For the conditional case, Node also supports a dynamic, function-like import('./math.js') (lowercase, with parentheses) that returns a Promise, a signal that this path is asynchronous by design, unlike require.

Require's synchronous, immediate-execution model has another consequence with **circular requires**: if module A requires module B, and B requires A (directly or through a longer chain) before A has finished its top-level code, B receives whatever partial module.exports A has built *so far*, not the finished version. That is rarely what anyone wants, and it's a CommonJS-specific problem; ESM's static, pre-resolved graph handles circular imports more gracefully through 'live bindings' that update once the exporting module finishes evaluating.

sections.heading: Configuring and Mixing the Two Systems
Which One Should You Actually Use?
sections.body: For new projects, ES Modules is where the ecosystem and the language are heading, and it's a reasonable default, partly because it unlocks top-level await (await directly in a module's top-level code, outside any async function, which CommonJS can't do). You will still spend a long time working with packages that ship as CommonJS, so understanding require()'s synchronous loading and circular-require quirks remains practical knowledge, not legacy trivia. The rule of thumb: pick one system per project, set it explicitly through package.json's "type" field rather than relying on the default, remember that on older Node versions a CJS project's require() can't pull in an ESM-only dependency without dynamic import(), and expect to translate import syntax when an npm package's documentation assumes ESM and your project is CommonJS.

examples.title: The Same Module, Written Both Ways
examples.explanation: Both versions produce the same result through different loading mechanisms. The CommonJS require call executes synchronously and can omit the file extension, because Node's CommonJS resolution tries .js, .json, and directory lookups automatically. The ESM import statement is statically resolved before any module code runs, and ESM resolution requires the full file extension (./mathUtils.mjs, not ./mathUtils); leaving it off is a common early mistake when switching from CommonJS habits. The .mjs extension also matters on its own: it forces that file to be an ES Module whatever the nearest package.json's "type" says, which is useful for adding a single ESM file to an otherwise CommonJS project. (The two halves above are separate files; in one file the duplicate `square` declarations would clash.)

examples.title: Circular require() and a Half-Finished module.exports
examples.explanation: require('./a') from main.js starts a.js running immediately and synchronously. a.js sets module.exports.value = 1, then requires b.js, which starts running in turn. When b.js requires('./a') partway through, a.js hasn't finished: it's paused mid-file, waiting on that very require('./b') call. Node doesn't re-run a.js from the top (that would recurse forever); it hands b.js whatever a.js's module.exports currently holds, which is { value: 1 }, since the assignment value = 2 later in a.js hasn't run. That's why b.js reports a.value as 1, not 2: circular requires get not a finished module but a snapshot of whatever partial state existed when the cycle closed. (The three files here are separate; run main.js.)

examples.title: Recovering __dirname in an ES Module
examples.explanation: import.meta.url gives this module's own location as a file:// URL string, which ESM provides natively, unlike Node's CommonJS-only __dirname. fileURLToPath (from Node's url core module) converts that URL into an ordinary OS-native path, and path.dirname strips the filename, giving the value __dirname would have held in a CommonJS file. process.cwd() is not a substitute: it returns the directory the process was launched *from*, which in any project with real folder structure is often not where this source file lives, so relying on it breaks as soon as someone runs the app from a different working directory. On Node 20.11 and later, import.meta.dirname gives the same value in one step.

misconceptions.description: require() and import are just two different pieces of syntax for doing the exact same thing under the hood, so which one a file uses is purely a style preference.
misconceptions.clarification: They differ in ways beyond syntax. require loads and executes synchronously at the call site and can be called conditionally anywhere; import is statically resolved and loaded asynchronously, must appear at a module's top level, and enables tooling (bundling, tree-shaking) that inspects the dependency graph without running code. They also differ on live bindings: ESM's imported names are live, read-only views onto the exporting module's values that update if the export changes later, while a destructured CommonJS require result is a one-time snapshot taken at require time.

misconceptions.description: Since Node supports both module systems, you can require() any ES Module file the same way you require() a CommonJS one, and vice versa, without any special handling.
misconceptions.clarification: The interop is asymmetric. ESM can import a CommonJS module fairly transparently, since Node treats the CJS module's module.exports as its default export. Going the other way is restricted: require() is synchronous and ESM loading is asynchronous by design, so on older Node versions require() of an ES Module throws ERR_REQUIRE_ESM. Node 22.12 and later allow it when the ESM graph has no top-level await (otherwise ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE). The dynamic, Promise-returning import() works from CommonJS on every version.

exercises.prompt: Given these two CommonJS files, what gets logged, and in what order, when main.js runs require('./a')?
hints: Trace execution top to bottom starting from main's require('./a'). a.js starts running immediately, before main.js's next line.
When b.js requires a.js partway through, a.js hasn't finished running yet -- what does Node hand back in that situation: a fully finished module.exports, or whatever a.js has built up so far?
module.exports.value = 1 has already run in a.js before it requires b.js -- so that partial value IS visible to b.js, even though a.js's LATER line (value = 2) hasn't executed yet at that point.
exercises.expectedAnswer: 'a.js starts', 'b.js starts', 'b.js sees a.value = 1', 'a.js sees b.value = 20', 'main.js sees a.value = 2'. b.js sees a's partially built exports (value=1) rather than a's final value of 2.
exercises.solutionExplanation: main.js's require('./a') starts a.js: it logs 'a.js starts', sets module.exports.value = 1, then calls require('./b'), which starts b.js. b.js logs 'b.js starts', sets its own value to 10, then calls require('./a'), but a.js is still paused at that require('./b') line, so Node hands back a.js's current, unfinished exports object, { value: 1 }. b.js logs that as 1, sets its value to 20, and finishes, returning { value: 20 } to a.js's require('./b') call. a.js resumes, logs b.value as 20 (b.js had completely finished by then), sets its own value to 2, and finishes. Finally main.js's require('./a'), which had been waiting, resolves to a.js's finished exports, { value: 2 }, so main.js logs 2.

exercises.prompt: A CommonJS Node project (no 'type' field in package.json) has this file, and running it with node app.js on an older Node version (before 22.12; newer versions can load this particular file) fails immediately with 'Error [ERR_REQUIRE_ESM]: require() of ES Module ... not supported'. Find and fix the problem in a way that works on every version, assuming logger.mjs must stay written as an ES Module.
hints: require() is synchronous. Could it load an ES Module file (.mjs) at all on older Node versions?
Node provides another way to load an ES Module from CommonJS code, one that's asynchronous and returns something you have to await or .then() rather than the exports themselves.
Since dynamic import() returns a Promise, the code that uses it will need to either live inside an async function, or use .then(), rather than a single synchronous top-level require line.
exercises.solutionExplanation: On older Node versions require() cannot load an ES Module: require is synchronous and ESM loading is asynchronous by design. (Node 22.12 and later relax this for ES modules without top-level await, but the fix below works everywhere, including for ESM that uses top-level await.) The fix is Node's dynamic import() function, which is legal to call from CommonJS files and returns a Promise. Because it's asynchronous, it must be awaited, here inside an async main() wrapper since top-level await isn't available in CommonJS files, rather than assigned directly the way require's result is. Once awaited it gives back the same { log } exports object a static import would have given in an ESM file.

assessments.prompt: Why did a CommonJS file historically fail to require() an ES Module (and why does it still fail for one that uses top-level await), while an ES Module can import a CommonJS module without much trouble?
options: It's an arbitrary restriction Node added; there's no technical reason it couldn't work in both directions.

require() is synchronous and returns its result immediately on the same line, but loading an ES Module is inherently asynchronous -- there's no way to synchronously hand back a result that isn't ready yet. ESM's import (dynamic or static) is asynchronous by design, so it can wait for a CommonJS module's already-synchronous load to finish without any conflict.
ES Modules can only be loaded in a browser, never inside a Node.js process directly.
CommonJS modules are always smaller in file size, so they load fast enough for import to handle them, while ES Modules are too large for require to process.
assessments.explanation: The constraint is technical, about loading semantics. require's contract is to hand back a finished result synchronously on the line it's called, and that can't be done for a module graph that loads asynchronously, such as one with top-level await. (Node 22.12 and later can require() an ES module with no top-level await, because such a graph can be evaluated synchronously.) Import is asynchronous by design, so it has no trouble waiting on a CommonJS module's load, which is synchronous and instant from import's perspective. The “It's an arbitrary restriction Node added; there's…” option is wrong because this is a real technical constraint. The “CommonJS modules are always smaller in file…” option is wrong: file size has nothing to do with it. The “ES Modules can only be loaded…” option is wrong: Node has run ESM files directly, with no browser, since roughly version 12-13.

assessments.prompt: A .js file lives in a project whose package.json has no "type" field at all. How does Node decide whether to treat that file as CommonJS or an ES Module?
options: Omitting the "type" field defaults to CommonJS, so the .js file is loaded and executed as CommonJS.
Node refuses to run the file at all until "type" is set explicitly to either value.
Node inspects the file's contents for import/export keywords and automatically picks the matching module system.
Node treats it as an ES Module by default, mirroring how a browser's <script type="module"> behaves.
assessments.explanation: Node decides a .js file's module system from the nearest package.json's "type" field, and the documented default when the field is omitted is "commonjs", so a .js file in a project with no "type" field is loaded as CommonJS, require/module.exports and all. The “Node inspects the file's contents for import/export…” option is wrong: Node doesn't scan file contents to infer the module system; it relies on the "type" field (or the .mjs/.cjs extension). Recent Node versions do add a fallback that re-parses an ambiguous file as ESM when CommonJS parsing fails on import/export syntax, but that is a fallback, not how the module system is chosen, and an explicit "type" avoids it. The “Node treats it as an ES Module…” option is wrong: CommonJS remains the default for backwards compatibility with the existing ecosystem. The “Node refuses to run the file…” option is wrong: omitting "type" is valid and extremely common.

assessments.prompt: The CommonJS example imports square via require('./mathUtils') (no extension), while the ES Module version needs import { square } from './mathUtils.mjs' (full extension included). Why does ESM require the extension while CommonJS can omit it?
options: It's arbitrary; both systems could equally support either behavior.
.mjs files cannot have their extension omitted because they are always precompiled ahead of time, unlike ordinary .js files.
CommonJS's require() runs its own resolution algorithm that automatically tries several extensions and directory-based lookups.
Node only added extension-omission support to CommonJS in a later version, and deliberately never backported it to ESM for security reasons.
assessments.explanation: require()'s resolution algorithm is forgiving: it tries appending .js and .json, and checks for a directory with an index file, if a specifier doesn't resolve directly. ESM's resolution has no equivalent step; specifiers must be exact, extension included, which helps resolve the whole dependency graph up front without running code. The “It's arbitrary; both systems could equally support either behavior” option dismisses a documented difference in resolution algorithms. The “.mjs files cannot have their extension omitted…” option invents a compilation distinction that isn't the reason. The “Node only added extension-omission support to CommonJS…” option fabricates a security-motivated history; the difference is resolution algorithm design.

assessments.prompt: Which statement about recovering __dirname-equivalent behavior inside an ES Module is correct?
options: __dirname is automatically available in ESM files too, since Node injects it as a global regardless of which module system is in use.
process.cwd() is a reliable substitute for __dirname, since it always returns the directory containing the currently executing module file.
There is no way to determine a module's own file location from within an ES Module; the value must be hardcoded or passed in as a parameter.
import.meta.url gives the current module's own location as a file:// URL string.
assessments.explanation: import.meta.url is the ESM-native primitive that exposes a module's own location as a file:// URL. Running it through fileURLToPath (from Node's 'url' core module) converts that URL to an OS-native path, and path.dirname on the result gives what __dirname would have given in CommonJS. The “process.cwd() is a reliable substitute for __dirname…” option is a common but wrong assumption: process.cwd() returns wherever the process was launched from, often not the directory of the source file, so file-relative paths break when the launch directory changes. The “__dirname is automatically available in ESM files…” option is wrong: __dirname is a CommonJS-only convenience that doesn't exist in ESM scope. The “There is no way to determine…” option is wrong: import.meta.url plus the reconstruction is the standard idiom for this.

assessments.prompt: A junior developer converted their Node project from CommonJS to ES Modules by changing package.json's 'type' field to 'module' and swapping require/module.exports for import/export. Afterward, every file that used __dirname to build file paths started throwing 'ReferenceError: __dirname is not defined'. Explain what happened and how to fix it properly.
assessments.modelAnswer: __dirname (along with __filename, require, module, and exports) is not part of the JavaScript language's ES Module specification. It's a convenience Node injects into CommonJS modules as part of its own implementation of that system. When package.json switched to "type": "module", every .js file in the project began loading as an ES Module, and Node doesn't define those CommonJS-only names there, so any code still referencing __dirname throws a ReferenceError. The name doesn't exist in an ES Module's scope; it isn't a usage mistake. The fix is to reconstruct the information from ESM's own primitive: import.meta.url gives the current module's location as a file:// URL string; fileURLToPath (from Node's 'url' core module) converts it into an OS-native filesystem path, and path.dirname of that result is the equivalent of __dirname. (On Node 20.11 and later, import.meta.dirname gives it in one step.) It's a few more lines than CommonJS's free global, but it's the standard idiom, and worth explaining to the junior developer that it isn't a gap Node forgot to fill: ESM is a language-level standard that doesn't bake in Node-specific globals the way Node's older CommonJS system did.
